recent_posts.title: Obsidian For Learning II: Process
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide to processing raw notes into atomic notes using Obsidian and the Zettelkasten method. Covers the daily workflow of converting fleeting notes and literature highlights into self-contained atomic notes with high cohesion and low coupling. Introduces a spaced repetition-based approach to managing the fleeting note backlog, explains how to organize atomic notes using an 'up' property to build a navigable tree structure, and demonstrates the full processing pipeline from capture to atomic note creation.

recent_posts.title: Using powerlifting to prevent desk work injuries
recent_posts.summary: Powerlifting offers a time-efficient solution to repetitive strain injuries and posture problems caused by desk work. The three core compound lifts (squat, press, deadlift) train the entire body in just 30 minutes, 3 times per week, strengthening muscles, ligaments, and bones that deteriorate from prolonged sitting and typing. Unlike ergonomic adjustments or daily stretching routines, powerlifting builds foundational strength that prevents injuries rather than merely managing symptoms. Novice lifters can expect rapid progress in the first year, gaining approximately 80% of their total lifting capacity primarily through nervous system adaptation rather than muscle growth.

recent_posts.title: Understanding Rust's compile time macros and const functions
recent_posts.summary: Explores Rust's compile-time capabilities through const functions and macros, demonstrating how arbitrary code execution during compilation enables powerful metaprogramming. Covers the differences between const functions (limited, pure subset) and macros (full language access), practical applications like reducing boilerplate, and addresses security concerns around compile-time code execution. Argues that Rust's first-class macro system is a feature, not a vulnerability, drawing parallels to Lisp's 70-year-old approach to compile-time computation.

recent_posts.title: Using Obsidian for accelerated learning and knowledge management
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to using Obsidian as a knowledge management system for accelerated learning. Covers the fundamentals of linking notes, using tags instead of folders, leveraging search and bookmarks, and implementing a three-part capture system for lecture notes, literature highlights, and fleeting thoughts. Introduces the 'temporal contract' concept for managing ideas across time and demonstrates practical setup using plugins like ReadWise for literature capture and Quick Add for thought capture.

recent_posts.title: Why async Rust breaks the borrow checker and what to do about it
recent_posts.summary: Async programming in Rust, particularly with Tokio, forces developers to use static lifetimes which effectively disables much of Rust's borrow checker benefits. The author argues that while async Rust is powerful, it breaks Rust's core promise of fearless concurrency through compile-time guarantees. Solutions include using scoped approaches, alternative runtimes like smol, or sticking with native threads and libraries like rayon for parallelism when async isn't strictly necessary.

recent_posts.title: 30 rust-powered tools to enhance your command line
recent_posts.summary: This post introduces 30 Rust-powered command line tools that offer modern, efficient replacements and enhancements for traditional utilities. It highlights tools like Uutills, Fish shell, and FD, focusing on their features, improvements, and compatibility. Additionally, it shares updates and advice for using these tools to optimize command line interactions.

recent_posts.title: Writing at the Speed of Thought
recent_posts.summary: Tris, a writer of various forms including technical videos and fiction podcasts, shares insights on how writing systems enhance thinking and reasoning. Inspired by George Orwell's '1984', he emphasizes the importance of editing in the writing process, suggesting that our current tools are not optimized for editing. Highlighting Vim's command mode as a solution, Tris advocates for its implementation to speed up both editing and thinking. Vim mode offers a seamless editing experience across multiple applications, supporting a more efficient and thoughtful workflow.

recent_posts.title: Why Rust is the future of programming
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses the evolution and significance of the C programming language, highlighting its enduring impact across various applications from the 1970s to today. It draws a parallel with Rust, positioning Rust as the modern successor to C due to its low-level portability, compatibility, and efficiency. The author argues that learning Rust now could offer a similar career stability and flexibility as C did for developers in the past.

recent_posts.title: Obsidian: The Good Parts
recent_posts.summary: Learn how to maximize the features of Obsidian for building a custom, flexible second brain. Discover the importance of using tags and links over folders, and how Obsidian's properties and Named Links can enhance the organization and retrieval of your information. This guide highlights best practices and common pitfalls to avoid, ensuring you can create a robust and scalable knowledge system.

recent_posts.title: AI is not Designed for You
recent_posts.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, including Apple's new AI, often fall short of the lofty promises made by companies. The initial hype around AI tends to focus on capabilities seen in movies, like general intelligence, but real-world applications are usually more mundane and limited. Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are good for surface-level tasks but struggle with deeper, more specific queries. The overpromises are largely driven by the need to impress investors rather than actual functionality improvements. The post emphasizes understanding AI's current practical capabilities and not getting caught up in future promises.
